summary: This document defines a YANG data model for configuring and managing routing policies in a vendor-neutral way. The model offers a generic routing policy framework that can be extended for specific routing protocols with the YANG augment mechanism.

eli5.summary: Routers follow rules about which routes to accept or prefer. This document defines a common form to write those rules, so the same form can work for many different brands.

questions: what is a yang routing policy model
how does routing policy evaluation work
subtitle: A vendor-neutral YANG model for the rules routers use to accept, reject and tweak routes.

tldr.problem: Operators with routers from several vendors need a consistent way to configure routing policy, but each vendor expresses policy differently.
tldr.mechanism: The ietf-routing-policy YANG module describes policies as ordered statements of conditions and actions, built on reusable prefix, neighbor and tag sets. Routing protocol models can add their own conditions and actions with YANG augment.
tldr.outcome: It is a generic base, not a complete feature set. Protocol-specific policy such as BGP is left to other models that extend it.

today: RFC 9067 is a Proposed Standard from October 2021. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it is meant to be used with routing protocol models such as BGP.

sections.title: Why a Routing Policy Model
sections.content:
This document defines a YANG data model for routing policy configuration, based on operational usage and best practices in a variety of service provider networks. It is meant to be vendor neutral, so operators can manage policy consistently when routers come from multiple vendors. The modules conform to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA).

The model does not aim to be feature complete. It is a subset of what vendors offer, covering widely used constructs for how routes are imported, exported and modified across routing protocols. Items found in only one implementation are left out, with the expectation that vendor modules will augment the model.

The design reflects an observation that a simple condition-action approach maps readily to several vendor implementations and gives operators a familiar way to express policy. A side effect is that other methods of expressing policy are not considered.
sections.eli5: Different brands of router speak different dialects for the same rules. This gives them one shared way to write the rules down.

sections.title: Model Overview
sections.content:
The module has three main parts. First, a generic framework expresses policies as sets of related conditions and actions, with match sets and actions that are useful across many routing protocols. Second, a structure lets protocol models add protocol-specific conditions and actions through YANG augmentations. A BGP example appears in a proposed vendor-neutral BGP model, and Appendix A shows how such an augmentation could look, though it is not normative. Third, a reusable grouping attaches import and export rules in the context of routing configuration for different protocols, Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) instances and so on.

Three terms matter. A routing policy defines how routes are imported, exported, modified and advertised. A policy statement is a set of conditions and actions, either of which may be empty. A policy chain is a sequence of policy definitions that can be referenced from different contexts.
sections.eli5: There is a basic rulebook everyone shares, a way for each routing protocol to add its own pages, and a way to hand the rulebook to a router.

sections.title: Defined Sets, Conditions and Actions
sections.content:
Policies are a sequence of top-level policy definitions. Each has a sequence of statements, and each statement is a condition-action tuple. Conditions can include several match or comparison operations. Actions can change route attributes or give a final disposition of accepting or rejecting the route.

The model provides generic defined sets that conditions can match against. A prefix set holds IP prefixes, each with a netmask range or exact length. A neighbor set holds neighboring nodes by IP address and selects routes by who advertised them. A tag set holds generic tag values.

Matches can be modified with match-set-options: all (true only if the value matches every member), any (true if it matches any member) and invert (true if it matches no member). Not every option suits every set, so the model restricts them where needed. The generic conditions include calling another policy, testing the source protocol, and matching an interface, prefix set, neighbor set, tag set or route type.

Generic actions are policy-result (accept or reject), setting a metric, metric type, route level, route preference, tag and application tag. Most conditions and actions are expected to come from protocol models via augmentation.
sections.eli5: You make lists, such as addresses you trust. A rule says: if a route is on this list, then accept it or change it.

sections.title: How Policies Are Evaluated and Applied
sections.content:
Statements in a definition are evaluated in the order defined. When all the conditions of a statement hold, its actions run. If those actions include accept-route or reject-route, evaluation of that definition stops, and later policies in the chain are not evaluated. If no condition in a definition matches, evaluation moves to the next definition in the chain. At the end of the chain the default route disposition applies, which is reject-route unless the chain specifies another default.

A policy statement can call another policy like a subroutine. An accept-route result in the called policy counts as a true condition for the caller, and reject-route counts as false. A subroutine cannot itself accept or reject a route. That is decided only by the top-level policy. The model sets no nesting depth, but discourages nesting beyond a small number of levels (the text suggests two to three), and implementations MUST validate that there is no recursion among nested policies.

Whether conditions see the original or already-modified attributes depends on the implementation-specific match-modified-attributes leaf.

Policy is applied through an apply-policy grouping that other models can reuse. It has import and export policy chains plus default import and default export dispositions, and the defaults are to reject the route.
sections.eli5: The router reads the rules top to bottom. The first rule that matches decides yes or no, and if none match, the answer is no.

sections.title: Extending the Model
sections.content:
Appendix A shows how another data model can augment the routing policy model, using examples from a draft BGP model. It adds BGP defined sets such as community sets and AS path sets, plus BGP-specific conditions and actions. The RFC states this example is not normative with respect to that BGP model.

Appendix B gives XML examples. One defines a prefix set, a tag set and a policy that accepts routes matching both. Another selects OSPF intra-area and inter-area routes and exports them into IS-IS level 2.

The module also defines identities for metric types, route levels and route types covering OSPF, IS-IS and BGP, which protocol models can reference.
sections.eli5: The shared rulebook has blank pages at the back where each protocol can add its own special rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is accessed through management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF, with SSH and TLS as the mandatory-to-implement secure transports. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) can limit which users may read or write which nodes.

Writable nodes are sensitive because routing policy has a large effect on network operations. Changing prefix sets, neighbor sets, tag sets, conditions or actions could be used for a Denial-of-Service attack, to redirect or drop traffic, or to allow many routes to leak into a routing domain such as BGP. Changes to tag sets can be harder to spot than changes to prefix sets.

Read access also matters. Knowing the sets can reveal which prefixes or neighbors to attack, and the policies themselves may reveal partners, customers and suppliers or count as intellectual property.
sections.eli5: Whoever can edit the rules can steer the traffic, and even reading the rules tells secrets, so only trusted people should get access.
